title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
about:
To the Lighthouse follows the Ramsay family and their guests at a summer house on the Isle of Skye, looking across the bay to a lighthouse. In the first part, The Window, very little happens outwardly across a single afternoon and evening: six-year-old James longs to sail to the Lighthouse tomorrow and his father says the weather will not allow it; Mrs. Ramsay knits a stocking for the keeper's boy, tries to arrange a marriage, and presides over a long dinner; Lily Briscoe, a guest, struggles to paint Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window. The second part, Time Passes, moves through ten years in a few pages while the empty house decays. The third part, The Lighthouse, returns to the house, where the trip is finally made and Lily goes back to her unfinished picture.

Virginia Woolf published the novel in 1927, between Mrs. Dalloway and Orlando. She drew the Ramsays from her own parents, Leslie Stephen and Julia Stephen, and the setting from the family's summers at Talland House in St Ives, Cornwall, moved here to the Hebrides. The story is told almost entirely from inside its characters' minds, passing from one consciousness to the next, often within a paragraph, so that the same moment is seen by several people at once. What happens matters less than how it is perceived, remembered and made to last.

angleCards.title: Whose mind are we in?
angleCards.text: Woolf moves between characters without announcing it, sometimes in the middle of a sentence. Watch for the moments when the point of view passes from one person to another, and notice how differently each of them sees the same room, meal or glance.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track the shifts in point of view, noticing whose mind each passage belongs to and how the same moment looks from different people's positions.

angleCards.title: Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay.
angleCards.text: The book was drawn from Woolf's own parents, and it studies a marriage in close detail: the demands, the silences, the tenderness that is never said aloud. Read for what each of them needs from the other and what each refuses to give.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read To the Lighthouse as a portrait of a marriage, following what Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay ask of each other and what goes unsaid between them.

angleCards.title: Lily's painting.
angleCards.text: Lily Briscoe spends the book trying to get a picture right, against a man who tells her women can't paint. Follow her problem with the canvas, the mass on the right and the mass on the left, as a question about how art is made and who is allowed to make it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Lily Briscoe's painting as the book's argument about art, looking at what she is trying to see and what stands in her way.

angleCards.title: Time and what lasts.
angleCards.text: The middle of the novel compresses ten years into a few pages, and much of what happens to the family is reported in brackets. Notice how the book handles time: the long hours of a single evening, the years that pass in a line, and the moments someone tries to make permanent.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to pay attention to how the novel treats time and memory: what it slows down, what it rushes past, and what the characters try to hold on to.

cast.name: Mrs. Ramsay
cast.description: Mother of eight, hostess of the summer house, and the center around whom everyone else arranges themselves. She is admired, protective and managing, drawn to matchmaking and to private moments of stillness that none of her guests see.

cast.name: Mr. Ramsay
cast.description: A distinguished philosopher, and a demanding husband and father who insists on hard facts, even when they wound his son. He worries constantly whether his work will last and turns to his wife for reassurance.

cast.name: Lily Briscoe
cast.description: An unmarried painter spending the summer near the Ramsays, working on a picture of Mrs. Ramsay in the window. She watches the family with love and irritation, and doubts her own work against the voices that say women cannot paint.

cast.name: James Ramsay
cast.description: The youngest son, six years old, desperate to go to the Lighthouse the next day. His father's flat refusal to promise good weather fills him with a murderous fury, and the wish to make the trip runs through the whole book.

cast.name: William Bankes
cast.description: A widowed botanist and Mr. Ramsay's oldest friend, spending the summer nearby. Orderly and reserved, he quietly reveres Mrs. Ramsay and becomes Lily's companion on walks and a patient viewer of her picture.

cast.name: Charles Tansley
cast.description: One of Mr. Ramsay's students, poor, awkward and fiercely ambitious. The children mock him; Mrs. Ramsay protects him; and he tells Lily that women can't paint and women can't write.

whyItMatters.title: A Novel Made From Inside the Mind
whyItMatters.body: To the Lighthouse is one of the fullest demonstrations of what the modernist novel set out to do. Instead of a narrator reporting events, the book moves through the thoughts and perceptions of its characters, passing from one to another so that a dinner, a walk or a glance is experienced from several positions at once. Woolf's method makes the reader do some of the work, holding several partial views together. Readers used to a single narrating voice still find that the book trains a different kind of attention.

whyItMatters.title: A Portrait of Woolf's Own Family
whyItMatters.body: Woolf wrote the Ramsays out of her parents, Leslie and Julia Stephen, and the summers of her childhood at St Ives. Her sister Vanessa Bell wrote that the portrait of their mother was painfully close to the woman herself, and Woolf later said that writing the book laid the ghost of her mother to rest. The novel deals with the Victorian family from inside it: the father's need for praise, the mother's authority and self-sacrifice, the children's rage and love. The same questions about who gives and who takes in a household remain open.

whyItMatters.title: Who Gets To Make Art
whyItMatters.body: Lily Briscoe is the book's other center. She is a single woman with little money and no reputation, told by a young man at dinner that women can't paint and can't write, and the novel follows her across ten years as she tries to finish one picture on her own terms. Woolf would make the same argument directly two years later in A Room of One's Own. Lily's question of how to see clearly, and how to go on working when no one expects the work to matter, still applies to anyone making something in private.
